Simpson County sits in south central Kentucky near the Tennessee line, with Franklin as its county seat. The county clerk handles the sale of delinquent real property tax claims, which Kentucky calls certificates of delinquency. This guide explains how Simpson County tax sales work, when they are usually held, how registration works, what returns investors can expect, and what steps matter most before you spend money. It also points you to the main county and state sources for updates.

What is Simpson County’s Tax Lien Investing setup?

Simpson County sells tax lien certificates, not tax deeds at the initial sale. In Kentucky, unpaid real property taxes move from the sheriff to the county clerk and become certificates of delinquency. Those certificates are then sold to third party buyers. The buyer gets a tax lien claim and earns simple interest at 1 percent per month on the unpaid balance. Kentucky does not use a bid down interest system for this sale format.

Important Details

Key Takeaways

  • Simpson County, Kentucky, offers tax lien certificates, where buyers earn 1% simple interest monthly on unpaid balances.
  • Tax sales occur in August, requiring registration with the county clerk, and prioritize claims for prior year holders.
  • Due diligence is crucial for investors; verify property details and potential issues before making a purchase.
  • Kentucky allows out-of-state and foreign investors to participate in tax lien sales, provided they meet registration requirements.
  • OTC purchases give buyers a chance to buy unsold liens post-auction, allowing for more time to assess options.

Fun Facts About the County

  • Simpson County’s 2025 population estimate was 20,788. It was 19,594 in the 2020 Census.
  • The county seat is Franklin, which sits close to Interstate 65 and the Tennessee line.
  • Kentucky Downs and The Mint Gaming Hall are in Simpson County.
  • The county has a long record of local history shown at the Simpson County History Center and Old Jail.

Attractions & Economic Highlights

  • Attractions include Dueling Grounds Distillery, Simpson County History Center, Octagon Hall, and Kentucky Downs.
  • Transportation is helped by I 65 and CSX rail access.
  • The local economy benefits from manufacturing, logistics, retail, tourism, and gaming activity. This is based on the industrial authority and tourism profile.
  • Outdoor time, horse racing, bourbon stops, and small town downtown shopping add local appeal.

Why This County is Ideal for Tax Lien Investors

  • Simpson County sits in an active corridor near I 65, which helps support demand and local business activity.
  • Kentucky tax lien certificates earn 1% simple interest per month, which is higher than many savings products.
  • The sale process is rule based. That helps investors who like a clear system.
  • This can fit investors who want high returns with a lower entry cost than buying full properties at deed sales. That said, it is only low risk when you do good research first.

Auction Process for Tax Lien Sales

Simpson County follows Kentucky’s certificate of delinquency sale process. The county clerk advertises the sale and registers buyers. Buyers do not bid the interest rate down. Instead, they submit lists of the bills they want. Prior year holders get first claim on matching current year bills if they file on time. After those claims are sorted, the remaining bills are sold by random order and in set lot sizes.

How the Auction Works

Here is a simple look at how the Simpson County tax lien sale works from notice through post-sale rights.

  1. Register first

    Every bidder must register with the county clerk and submit the county form, fees, deposit, and state registration proof if needed.

  2. Submit your bill lists

    You list the certificates you want to buy. Simpson County also has a separate process for prior year holders.

  3. Bring deposit funds

    For current year bills, the county requires a 25% deposit on the total amount listed.

  4. Report on sale day

    Registered buyers report to the county clerk for instructions. The final list may change because owners can still pay right up to sale time.

  5. Priority claims go first

    If a buyer holds a valid prior year claim on the same property and filed on time, that claim is handled first.

  6. Random draw for the rest

    The clerk uses a random drawing to set selection order for the remaining bills.

Maximum Potential Returns and Expected Returns on Simpson County Tax Lien Certificates

The basic return is simple interest at 1 percent per month, which works out to 12 percent per year if the lien stays unpaid for a full year. That is the base yield many investors focus on. Your actual return depends on how fast the owner pays, how much capital sits idle before you deploy it, and what approved fees you may lawfully collect. If the lien is paid sooner, your total dollars earned will be lower, even though the monthly rate stays the same. If the lien goes unpaid long enough, Kentucky law allows collection or foreclosure action after one year from delinquency, which can change the risk and reward picture.

Open to All Investors and Foreign Investor Participation

Kentucky’s third party purchaser rules focus on registration thresholds, tax compliance, entity details, and purchase activity. The state pages do not limit participation to Kentucky residents. That means out of state buyers, business entities, and in many cases foreign backed entities can take part if they meet the state and county registration rules and provide the required paperwork. Buyers planning to purchase more than three certificates in one county, more than five statewide, or invest more than $10,000 must register with the Kentucky Department of Revenue before they can buy.

Importance of Due Diligence in Simpson County Tax Lien Investing

What Due Diligence Entails

  • Check the tax bill list and compare it with the PVA and county land records.
  • Verify mailing address, parcel number, and owner name before you fund your list.
  • Review mortgages, easements, court cases, and bankruptcy filings. Kentucky lien investing is still legal work if it goes to collection.
  • Inspect the area, access, and use of the parcel.
  • Know your notice duties after purchase.

Risks of Skipping Due Diligence

  • You may buy a weak lien on a hard to collect parcel.
  • You may miss title issues or owner insolvency.
  • You may misread what happens after one year.
  • You may overestimate resale or foreclosure value.
  • You may lose time and fee recovery if your notices are not done right.

Buying Over the Counter Liens in Simpson County

How to Purchase OTC Liens or Deeds

Kentucky allows unsold certificates to be purchased after the county sale. The state manual says any remaining certificates of delinquency may be purchased at any time by any third party after the sale is complete, subject to ongoing registration rules and per bill fees until the yearly cap is reached. Start with the Simpson County Clerk to ask what remains unsold and what paperwork is needed.

Benefits of OTC Purchases

OTC buying removes sale day pressure. You may get more time to review the bill list. You also avoid the random draw process used at the live county sale. The same state fee rules still apply.

Why Simpson County is a Top Choice for Tax Lien Investors

Economic and Tax Advantages

  • August sale timing is common in Simpson County and across Kentucky.
  • The county sits on a strong road and rail corridor.
  • Kentucky offers a clear lien sale process and a fixed monthly interest rate.

Real Estate Market Overview

Simpson County is not one of Kentucky’s largest counties, yet it shows steady population growth since 2020. That matters because population growth, transport access, and active local business can support housing demand and property turnover. For lien buyers, that does not remove risk, but it can improve the odds that a parcel has a real payer, real use, or real exit path.

Conclusion

Simpson County is a Kentucky tax lien certificate market. The sale is usually held in August. Registration is required. The county clerk is the main point of contact. The return is based on simple interest at 1 percent per month, not on a bid down rate. The process is more structured than many deed sales, with priority claims, deposits, and random selection for remaining bills. That can work well for investors who like rules and repeatable systems. Still, smart investing starts with strong research. Check the parcel, the owner, the records, and the state rules before you commit funds.

Pro Tips

  • Focus on parcels with clear mailing data and easy to trace ownership.
  • Check whether a bill may be paid off before sale day. The list can change fast.
  • In Simpson County, track August dates early. The exact day can shift year to year.
  • Use I 65 access as a quick screen for demand and usability in the area.
  • Ask the clerk whether any unsold certificates remain after the sale. OTC can give you more time to review.

FAQs for Simpson County Tax Liens

Do I get the property right away?

No. You buy a tax lien certificate, not immediate title.

Can I renovate a property after buying the lien?

Not unless you later gain title through the legal process.

Do mortgages vanish at the county sale?

No. This is a lien purchase stage, not an instant deed sale.

Can I finance my lien purchase?

The county requires approved funds for fees and deposits.

Do I need a quiet title right after the sale?

No. Quiet title issues matter later only if title is acquired through foreclosure or related court action.
